angora.origin: Angora is the hair of Angora breeds of the domestic rabbit, Oryctolagus cuniculus, kept for wool rather than meat or pelts. Studied lines include French Angoras and Chinese strains such as Zhexi and Wan, which dominate recent genetic research. The long coat has an identified genetic component: whole-genome resequencing found a missense substitution in the fibroblast growth factor 5 gene (Fgf5) homozygous in all Angora rabbits tested, which impairs FGF5 binding to its receptor FGFR1 and is associated with the long-hair trait. Angora is distinct from mohair, the hair of the Angora goat.
angora.structure: The Angora rabbit is double-coated: fine down fibers dominate numerically, with a minority of coarse bristle fibers, and breeders distinguish fine- and coarse-wool lines that differ in follicle density and fiber diameter. The fibers are keratin, and a ladder-like medulla is a classic microscopic feature of rabbit hair. In an optical analysis of 349 French Angora fleece samples, the mean comfort factor, the share of fibers at or below 30 microns, was 97.5%, and the measured medullated share was low at 0.1 to 7.3%, but the authors noted the instrument was not adapted to Angora medullas and needed special calibration. Fiber diameter increased with age.
angora.process: Angora is harvested several times a year by shearing, combing or plucking. Plucking removes hair loosened at the end of a growth cycle; in Wan strain rabbits, skin sampled after plucking showed follicles in telogen in the first week and in anagen from the fourth to the twenty-fourth week. Harvested fiber is sorted by length and bristle content, and because it is short, slippery and low in cohesion it is usually blended with other fibers such as wool before spinning. Nutrition matters: in one trial, methionine added to a low-protein diet restored wool yield that the low-protein diet had reduced.
angora.performance: Angora is very light and warm for its weight, and its slippery, low-friction surface lets fiber ends migrate out of the yarn, producing the characteristic halo but also shedding; blending reduces shedding while diluting the halo. It shares the hygroscopic, self-extinguishing behavior of keratin and dyes with acid dyes, though depth of shade can differ from wool in blends. Fabrics mat and felt under friction and moisture, so rubbing zones wear quickly. It is susceptible to clothes moth and carpet beetle larvae.
angora.identify: Burn tests (indicative only, and to be done with care) show ordinary keratin behavior. Under the microscope, rabbit hair shows a wide, ladder-like medulla, particularly in coarser fibers, together with fine diameters, which distinguishes it from sheep wool and goat fibers. MALDI-TOF peptide profiling has separated angora from cashmere, wool, mohair, yak, camel and alpaca, including dyed samples and 50% blends. No laboratory test reveals whether fiber was sheared, combed or plucked, so harvest claims depend on documentation.
angora.labeling: Angora rabbit hair is not a wool fiber under the US Wool Products Labeling Act. Under 16 CFR 303.6, the animal's name may be used with hair, fiber or blend when the fiber is 5% or more, and FTC guidance gives Angora Rabbit Hair as an acceptable disclosure; otherwise the term fur fiber may be used. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 reserves angora for angora rabbit hair, while other rabbit hair falls in the general animal hair category. Claims such as shorn only or no plucking are marketing representations that need supply-chain evidence.
angora.past: Angora rabbits have long been kept as specialist fiber animals, and veterinary literature from 1948 already discussed the effect of shearing Angora rabbits in bad weather on body temperature and health. Their breeding differs from sheep: a review of fiber genetics noted that several autosomal recessive genes govern rabbit coat traits, and that selecting double-coated Angoras on the single, easily measured trait of total fleece weight has also improved fleece quality. Recent Chinese programs apply genomic selection with imputed genome-wide markers and study follicle genes such as KRT17 and Wnt10b, while harvest method has become the central welfare and sourcing question for buyers.
